asymmetry, but with $k = 5$ it is severely underpowered and unstable; the "signal" is essentially the
single precise low-effect study C, and no conclusion about reporting bias is warranted from five trials.
The example shows both the mechanics and the fragility of the test.

**Decision impact: which interval, and why.** It is worth stating what a decision-maker would actually
conclude from these five trials, because the three analyses tell noticeably different stories. The
fixed-effect interval $0.266 \pm 1.96(0.069) = (0.130, 0.402)$ is the narrowest, but it excludes no
effect only because it *assumes* the five trials share one effect, which the $I^2$ of $30\%$ already
questions. The random-effects Wald interval $(0.127, 0.481)$ widens to admit heterogeneity, yet still
trusts a normal quantile and a plug-in $\tau^2$. The Hartung-Knapp interval $(0.058, 0.550)$ is wider
still and is the only one whose stated $95\%$ coverage survives having just $k = 5$ trials. All three keep
the effect positive here, but the *strength* of that conclusion weakens as the interval widens; a cautious
analyst reports the Hartung-Knapp interval and treats the fixed-effect interval as an optimistic bound.
This is the pattern to expect whenever heterogeneity is present and trials are few, which is the normal
situation in health technology assessment, and it is the same caution that will attend every indirect
comparison built on these pooled inputs.

## Notes and references {#sec-ma-notes}

This chapter expands items C.1 through C.9 of the companion proof catalogue into complete proofs in the
notation of this book, and adds the worked example and exercises. The primary reference for the
random-effects model, its estimation, and the Bayesian formulation is @dias2018nma, which is also the
source for the bridge from pairwise to network meta-analysis taken up in Chapters 14 and 15. The
method-of-moments heterogeneity estimator @eq-dl is from @dersimonian1986; we sharpened the catalogue's
asymptotic statement by proving exact unbiasedness of the untruncated estimator (@thm-dersimonian-laird),
which holds under second moments alone.

Further sources: @higgins2002 for $H^2$ and $I^2$ (@def-i-squared, @prp-i2-interpretation);
@hartung1999, @hartung2001, and @sidik2002 for the $t$ adjustment (@thm-hartung-knapp), with
@inthout2014 for its small-$k$ performance; @viechtbauer2005 and the `metafor` package
(@viechtbauer2010) for the REML estimating equation and its iterative solution (@thm-reml-tau2);
@egger1997 for the regression test (@thm-egger), with @sterne2001 and @stanley2014 (PET-PEESE) for the
complements noted there; @gelman2006 for half-normal and half-$t$ priors on $\tau$; and @veroniki2016
for a modern comparison of $\tau^2$ estimators.

The proofs lean on Part I: the Gauss-Markov theorem and the linear-model machinery (@thm-ols-blue,
@def-linear-model, @thm-ttest, @thm-sigma2-unbiased, @thm-rss-chisq, @lem-mvn-affine-closure) carry the
fixed-effect optimality, Cochran's $Q$, and the Hartung-Knapp result; the spectral theorem
(@thm-spectral-theorem) underlies @lem-projector-chisq; Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound
(@def-fisher-information, @thm-cramer-rao) give the efficiency of inverse-variance weighting; restricted
maximum likelihood (@def-reml, @thm-reml-one-sample) is specialized to the heterogeneity variance; and
normal-normal conjugacy (@thm-conjugate-normal) gives the Bayesian posterior. The random-effects model
@def-random-effects-ma is the meta-analytic case of the hierarchical construction @def-random-effects.

No result in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag. The companion Coq development under
`theories/` formalizes the identification and algebraic content of the indirect-comparison methods
(propensity scores, the Bucher contrast, outcome regression, doubly robust estimation, MAIC), not the
classical estimation theory of meta-analysis: there is no Coq counterpart to inverse-variance weighting,
Cochran's $Q$, or the heterogeneity-variance estimators, a scope decision recorded in the companion
manuscript. The cleanest candidates for future formalization are the purely algebraic identities here,
namely the best-linear-unbiased property of inverse-variance weights (@thm-fixed-effect-blue) and the
expected value of $Q$ (@prp-expected-q).

**Forward connections.** The fixed-effect contrast estimator and its variance @eq-ivw-var are the inputs
to the Bucher indirect comparison of Chapter 14 (@thm-bucher-unbiased) under the transitivity assumption
(@def-transitivity); the random-effects structure of @def-random-effects-ma becomes the multivariate
random effect of network meta-analysis, where contrasts sharing a comparator acquire the characteristic
correlation of @thm-re-nma-correlation; and Cochran's $Q$ generalizes to the network heterogeneity and
inconsistency statistics of Chapter 15. The within-study effects pooled here live on the linear-predictor
(link) scale, which is why their collapsibility properties (@def-collapsibility,
@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr) matter for what the pooled $\theta$ means.

## Exercises {#sec-ma-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have a complete worked solution in Appendix F. Start with the two
warm-ups, which need only the running example and a calculator; the later exercises build toward the
proofs.

::: {#exr-ma-warmup-weights}
## Which trial gets more weight? (warm-up)
Two trials estimate the same log odds ratio: trial $P$ reports $\hat\theta_P = 0.30$ with $s_P^2 = 0.01$,
and trial $R$ reports $\hat\theta_R = 0.10$ with $s_R^2 = 0.04$. (a) Compute the inverse-variance weights
$w_P$ and $w_R$, and state in words how many times more weight the more precise trial receives and why.
(b) Compute the fixed-effect estimate $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}$ and check that it lies closer to the more
precise trial. (c) Without recomputing from scratch, describe what happens to the two weights and to their
ratio if a heterogeneity variance $\tau^2 = 0.03$ is added to each $s_i^2$, and connect this to the
random-effects reweighting of Section @sec-ma-random.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-i2-interpretation}
## Interpreting $I^2$ (interpretation)
A meta-analysis of $k = 8$ trials reports $I^2 = 60\%$. For each statement, say whether it is true or
false and why. (a) "$60\%$ of the eight trials are biased." (b) "There is a $60\%$ probability that
heterogeneity is present." (c) "About $60\%$ of the observed variability among the estimates exceeds what
sampling error alone would produce." (d) "The pooled effect is wrong by $60\%$." (e) "A fixed-effect
analysis is therefore the safe choice." Justify each answer from @def-i-squared and @prp-i2-interpretation.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-fe-pipeline}
## Fixed-effect pipeline by hand ($\star$)
Three trials report a mean difference: $\hat\theta_1 = 1.2$ with $s_1^2 = 0.16$, $\hat\theta_2 = 0.8$
with $s_2^2 = 0.09$, $\hat\theta_3 = 1.5$ with $s_3^2 = 0.25$. (a) Compute the inverse-variance weights,
the fixed-effect estimate $\hat\theta_{\mathrm{FE}}$, and its standard error. (b) Compute Cochran's $Q$,
state its null distribution, and compute $I^2$. (c) Compute the constant $c$ of @eq-expected-q and the
DerSimonian-Laird estimate $\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}$. (d) Recompute the pooled estimate and its standard
error under the random-effects weights $\tilde w_i = 1/(s_i^2 + \hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}})$.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-cauchy-schwarz}
## Optimality and the equality case
Prove from scratch, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, that any linear unbiased estimator
$\sum_i a_i \hat\theta_i$ of $\theta$ under @eq-fe-model has variance at least $1/\sum_i w_i$, and that
equality holds if and only if $a_i = w_i/\sum_j w_j$. Then show, without Lagrange multipliers, that the
same conclusion follows by writing $a_i = w_i/W + d_i$ with $\sum_i d_i = 0$ and expanding the variance.
*Hint.* For the first route, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the vectors $(a_i s_i)_i$ and $(1/s_i)_i$ exactly as
in the remark after @thm-fixed-effect-blue. For the second, expand $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = \sum_i
a_i^2 s_i^2$ with $a_i = w_i/W + d_i$; the cross term vanishes because $\sum_i d_i = 0$, leaving $1/W$ plus
a nonnegative remainder $\sum_i d_i^2 s_i^2$ that is zero only when every $d_i = 0$.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-dl-unbiased}
## Exact unbiasedness and truncation bias of DerSimonian-Laird
(a) Using only the second-moment assumptions of @prp-expected-q, prove that the untruncated estimator
$\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = (Q - (k-1))/c$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] = \tau^2$.
(b) Deduce that the truncated estimator @eq-dl has $\mathbb{E}[\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}] \ge \tau^2$, with
strict inequality whenever $P(\tilde\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} < 0) > 0$. (c) Explain why the truncation bias is
largest when the true $\tau^2$ is near zero and negligible when $\tau^2$ is large.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-reml-balanced}
## REML reproduces the $(k-1)$ divisor ($\star$)
Suppose all within-study variances are equal, $s_i^2 \equiv s^2$. Starting from the REML estimating
equation @eq-reml-eqn, show that $\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}} = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i (\hat\theta_i -
\bar{\hat\theta})^2 - s^2$ (truncated at $0$), where $\bar{\hat\theta}$ is the unweighted mean. Compare
with the maximum likelihood estimator, which would divide by $k$, and explain the discrepancy in terms of
the degree of freedom spent on $\theta$, referencing @thm-reml-one-sample. *Hint.* Set all $\tilde w_i$
equal in @eq-reml-eqn; the right-hand side collapses to $(k-1)\tilde w$ and $\hat\theta_R$ becomes the
unweighted mean $\bar{\hat\theta}$, as in the equal-variance remark after @thm-reml-tau2.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-hk-scale}
## The Hartung-Knapp scale factor
Within the working model of @thm-hartung-knapp, let $q = \frac{1}{k-1}\sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i -
\hat\theta_R)^2$. (a) Show that $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HK}}(\hat\theta_R) = q\,
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R)$ with $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_R) = 1/\sum_i \tilde w_i$.
(b) Show $\mathbb{E}[q] = 1$ under the working model with $\sigma^2 = 1$, using
$(k-1)q = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2$ and @thm-cochran-q applied to the weights
$\tilde w_i$. (c) Explain why the Hartung-Knapp interval can be narrower than the Wald interval, and what
the $\max\{1, q\}$ safeguard does. *Hint for (b).* Under the working model with $\sigma^2 = 1$ the
variables $\sqrt{\tilde w_i}(\hat\theta_i - \theta)$ are standard normal, so
$(k-1)q = \sum_i \tilde w_i(\hat\theta_i - \hat\theta_R)^2$ is exactly the Cochran statistic of
@thm-cochran-q formed with the weights $\tilde w_i$, and that statistic has mean $k - 1$.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-bayes-shrinkage}
## Bayesian study-specific effects and shrinkage
In the random-effects model @eq-re-model with $\tau^2$ and $\theta$ known, derive the posterior of an
individual study effect $\theta_i$ given $\hat\theta_i$ using @thm-conjugate-normal, and show it is
$$
\theta_i \mid \hat\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}\big(B_i \theta + (1 - B_i)\hat\theta_i,\; (1 - B_i)s_i^2\big),
\qquad B_i = \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \tau^2}.
$$
Interpret $B_i$ as a shrinkage factor: less precise studies (large $s_i^2$) are pulled harder toward the
mean $\theta$. Connect this to the shrinkage estimator @thm-shrinkage-posterior-mean of Chapter 8.
:::

::: {#exr-ma-egger-identity}
## Egger's intercept as a weighted slope
For the data of @exr-ma-fe-pipeline, (a) fit Egger's regression @eq-egger and report $\hat\alpha$ and its
$t$ statistic on $k - 2 = 1$ degree of freedom. (b) Fit the precision-weighted regression of $\hat\theta_i$
on $s_i$ with weights $1/s_i^2$, and verify numerically that its slope equals $\hat\alpha$ and its
intercept equals $\hat\beta$, as @thm-egger asserts. (c) Comment on why a test on a single residual degree
of freedom is uninformative. *Hint.* Reuse the algebraic identity of @thm-egger: Egger's regression and
the weighted regression of $\hat\theta_i$ on $s_i$ minimize the same objective, so their fitted
coefficients swap roles. With $k = 3$ points and $p = 2$ parameters there are $k - 2 = 1$ residual degrees
of freedom.
:::
